I am 48 years old, and I have farmed these six mu of land in Quzhou since I left school at fifteen. My father taught me, and over the years I have learned what works here. The land is flat, the soil is loamy, and I have a well for irrigation, but water and labor are getting expensive, so I do not waste either.

It is late April now. My winter wheat is already in the field — I sowed it last October after rotary tillage, using an improved variety that I have grown for several years. The crop is at the jointing stage and looks green and full. I will topdress nitrogen once more, irrigate two more times before harvest, and spray for aphids and fusarium head blight. I do not gamble with new crops; wheat has a stable price and the grain station comes to the village to buy it.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I will plant summer corn immediately on the same land. I will use no-tillage planting to save time and soil moisture — every day counts because the corn needs enough growing degree-days before autumn frost. I will buy hybrid seed, probably Nongda 372 or Zhengdan 958, which gives me about 600 kg per mu if the weather cooperates. I will fertilize at sowing and topdress at the jointing or big-flare stage, irrigate three times, and control weeds and corn borers with two or three sprayings. I thought about planting cotton or watermelon on a small plot, but my son and daughter work in Shijiazhuang now, and it is just me and my wife. We cannot take the risk of a crop that needs daily tending and has a fickle market. Wheat and corn may not make me rich, but they put money in my pocket reliably.
